identification.summary: Dragos tracks CHERNOVITE as the developers of PIPEDREAM, a modular ICS attack framework that Dragos identified in early 2022 and described as the seventh known ICS-specific malware [S1][S5]. Mandiant tracks the same toolset as INCONTROLLER [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Dragos says it has tracked CHERNOVITE since 2021; PIPEDREAM was identified in early 2022 and publicly disclosed in April 2022 [S5][S1].
identification.notes: CHERNOVITE is Dragos's name for the toolset developers, not a Microsoft-named actor, so no Microsoft name is listed. Mandiant said it could not associate INCONTROLLER with any previously tracked group [S2]. Whether CHERNOVITE overlaps any other vendor's cluster (for example Sandworm or Microsoft's Seashell Blizzard) is not established in the sources gathered.

attribution.confidence: Dragos assesses with high confidence that CHERNOVITE is a state actor [S1]. Dragos states it does not conduct political attribution [S1]. Mandiant stated it believes the toolset was developed by a state-sponsored actor and found evidence of a possible Russia nexus, while its investigation was ongoing [S2][S4]. The April 2022 US government advisory did not attribute the tools to a country [S5].
attribution.basis: Vendor assessments only (Dragos, Mandiant) based on analysis of the tool capabilities [S1][S2][S4]. No government attribution to a named state organization was found in the sources gathered [S5].

objectives: Dragos assesses PIPEDREAM was built for disruptive or destructive operations against industrial control systems [S1]. Dragos said one potential use would be to disable an emergency shutdown system [S5]. Mandiant described capabilities related to disruption, sabotage and potentially physical destruction [S2]. Intended political or military purpose is not stated by the vendors [S1].

sectors: Industrial control systems broadly (Schneider Electric and Omron controllers, OPC UA servers)
targeting.notes: Dragos says initial targeting appears specific to LNG and electric power, but the framework works across a wide variety of industrial controllers [S1]. It first targets Schneider Electric and Omron controllers, not because of product-specific vulnerabilities [S1]. Mandiant said the malware posed the greatest risk to Ukraine and nations responding to the Russian invasion [S5]. No confirmed victims are public; CISA said it was not aware of the malware being used in the wild [S5].

capabilities.summary: PIPEDREAM lets operators scan for new devices, brute-force passwords, sever connections and crash target devices, using protocols including FINS, Modbus and Schneider Electric's CoDeSys implementation [S1]. Dragos describes it as modular, with five components [S1]. Mandiant describes INCONTROLLER as three tools: TAGRUN (scans for OPC servers, enumerates tags, brute-forces credentials, reads and writes tag values), CODECALL (Modbus and CODESYS framework with modules for at least three Schneider Electric PLCs) and OMSHELL (scans and interacts with some Omron PLCs over HTTP, Telnet and FINS, and Omron servo drives) [S2]. The joint US advisory said the modular design lets lower-skilled actors emulate more advanced ones, and noted a Windows component exploiting the ASRock driver AsrDrv103.sys (CVE-2020-15368) on engineering workstations [S3]. The tools operate after initial access to the OT network is established [S3]. The initial access method is not described in the sources gathered.

campaigns.name: PIPEDREAM / INCONTROLLER public disclosure
campaigns.summary: DOE, CISA, NSA and FBI issued advisory AA22-103A on 13 April 2022 on APT tools targeting ICS/SCADA devices, with Dragos and Mandiant assisting [S3][S5]. Dragos published its CHERNOVITE/PIPEDREAM analysis and Mandiant published its INCONTROLLER report the same period [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: No deployment observed
campaigns.summary: Dragos said PIPEDREAM had not yet been deployed in the wild for destructive effects and that it was found before deployment by the adversary [S1][S5]. CISA and partners said they were not aware of use in the wild [S5].

diamond.adversary: Developers of PIPEDREAM, assessed by Dragos with high confidence to be a state actor; Mandiant sees a possible Russia nexus [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: PIPEDREAM / INCONTROLLER modular ICS framework with OPC UA, Modbus, CODESYS and FINS interaction, plus an ASRock driver exploit component [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.victim: LNG and electric power equipment, Schneider Electric and Omron controllers, OPC UA servers; no confirmed victims [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Released during the Russian invasion of Ukraine; Mandiant said Ukraine and responding nations faced the greatest risk. Dragos does not make political attribution [S1][S5].
diamond.technology: Standard ICS protocols and native controller functionality rather than product-specific vulnerabilities, so patching alone does not remove the exposure [S1].

gaps: Dragos pages (dragos.com) could not be fetched; Dragos statements come from search-result excerpts, not full text. The Dragos CHERNOVITE whitepaper was not opened.
The Mandiant and CISA AA22-103A primary documents were not opened; they are used via search excerpts and secondary coverage (Security Affairs, SecurityWeek, TechTarget).
Initial access methods, infrastructure, and any victims are not public in the sources gathered.
Sponsor and country are unattributed by Dragos and the US advisory; Mandiant's Russia nexus was preliminary. Overlap with other tracked Russian clusters is unverified.
Dragos MOUSEHOLE deep-dive and runtime-testing posts were seen in search results but not opened or dated, so they are not cited.
Activity after April 2022 was not researched in detail.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is OT networks and engineering workstations controlling Schneider Electric and Omron PLCs, OPC UA servers, and LNG and electric power facilities [S1][S3]. STEP 2: The tools abuse standard ICS protocols and native functionality, so exposure is architectural, not patch-driven [S1]. STEP 3: The framework is used after OT network access is established, via modular scan, credential brute-force and device-manipulation tools [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is pre-positioning and reconnaissance of energy OT networks with no immediate effect. MDCOA is use of the toolkit to crash controllers or disable safety systems at an energy facility during a crisis [S1][S5]. Candidate indicators: OPC UA, Modbus, CODESYS or FINS scanning and brute-force from unusual hosts, loading of the AsrDrv103.sys driver on engineering workstations, and controller connection severing [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track OT protocol anomaly detection at supported energy infrastructure and share indicators from the joint advisory [S3]. (2) Authorities: OT monitoring and response on installation or contractor-owned industrial systems depends on owner authorities; confirm responsibilities in advance. (3) Mission assurance: identify mission-essential installations whose power and fuel depend on Schneider or Omron controlled systems and plan manual fallback. (4) Coordination: the original advisory was a DOE, CISA, NSA and FBI product developed with vendors, so coordinate through those channels and vendor partners [S3][S5].
